extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of evolutionary biology; readers evaluating theories of organic evolution
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for judging explanations of organic evolution, especially the adequacy of natural selection vs inheritance of functionally-produced (use/disuse) modifications. Focuses on evidential, mechanistic, and probabilistic demands placed on proposed evolutionary mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diminution by disuse as causal explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: The diminution of size which results from diminished use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observed reductions in structures of pampered lap-dogs (pug, toy-terrier, King Charles's spaniel) cannot be ascribed to artificial selection, natural selection, or economy of nutrition; these diminutions are best explained by inherited effects of disuse. Evidence: skull morphology (narrow zygomatic arches, reduced temporal fossae, weak muscle attachments) across many generations despite abundant feeding and lack of selective pressure. The text explicitly rules out other causes before attributing change to diminished use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement for coordinated change among co-operative parts
rubrics_metrics.description: To acquire some structure specially and largely developed, it is almost indispensable that several other parts should be modified and co-adapted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin's quoted principle: large specialised structures (e.g., elk horns, giraffe neck) require many accompanying modifications (bones, muscles, blood-vessels, nerves, thorax, fore-legs). The author argues that natural selection acting on isolated favourable variations cannot plausibly produce the multitude of coordinated adjustments required for complex co-adapted systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concomitant (coordinated) variation cannot be assumed
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when cooperative parts are closely united, nothing implies that they necessarily vary together; we are forbidden to assume that they vary together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples where co-operative parts do not vary together: cave blind crabs (lost eyes but retained stalks), pigeons (beak length changed without proportional tongue change), teeth and jaws in humans (jaws decreased, teeth did not). This undermines the assumption that selection can reliably change many cooperating parts in a coordinated way.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inheritance of functionally-produced modifications needed to explain coordinated re-adjustments
rubrics_metrics.description: If the effects of use and disuse of parts are inheritable, then changes in one set of parts will simultaneously cause by greater or less exercise a re-moulding of co-operative parts, generation after generation progressively fitting the whole structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied to the giraffe: inherited effects of altered function could progressively fit hind-quarters, vascular and nervous systems, and nutritional appliances to the increasing fore-quarters and neck. Without inheritance of functionally-produced changes, required re-adjustments cannot be made stepwise without fatal disadvantages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probability/feasibility constraint on selection producing many simultaneous favorable variations
rubrics_metrics.description: Considering how immense must be the number of required changes, the chances against any adequate re-adjustments fortuitously arising must be infinity to one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author enumerates the many distant and indirect changes (bones, muscles, blood supply, nerves, central tracts) that would be required to accommodate a major primary change; argues it is implausible that natural selection could wait until all appropriate secondary variations arose without the variety dying out from intermediate disadvantage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural selection limited in producing specialised minor/aesthetic faculties in complex organisms
rubrics_metrics.description: As the number of bodily and mental faculties increases, the production of specialities of character by natural selection alone becomes difficult; minor traits (e.g., aesthetic faculties) are especially unlikely to have evolved solely by natural selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: when many attributes contribute to survival, a superiority in any one attribute may not be sufficiently decisive to be increased by selection because individuals with ordinary levels can survive by other superiorities. Applied examples: musical faculty in humans, the diffusion of musical appreciation in Europeans compared with remote ancestors; prominent composers often did not leave more descendants, so selection is unlikely to explain musical endowment without inheritance of functional effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domestication produces broad variability that must be actively preserved
rubrics_metrics.description: Indefinite and almost illimitable variability is the usual result of domestication ... any particular variation would generally be lost by crossing, reversion, and accidental destruction ... unless carefully preserved by man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin quote and commentary: under domestication many variations appear and reappear but are not stable unless actively preserved. The contrast with mankind (not under a preserving agency) is used to argue why useful minor variations would disappear under natural selection alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accumulation of effects from changed conditions across generations implies inheritance of functional modifications
rubrics_metrics.description: The power of changed conditions accumulates; so that two, three, or more generations must be exposed to new conditions before any effect is visible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This observation implies that some change of constitution occurs over exposed generations, interpreted as modifications of organs adapting them to changed functions and being inherited. The text uses this to argue that changed functions register in reproductive elements and are subsequently manifested in offspring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correlated variation via functional modification
rubrics_metrics.description: When one part is modified through continued selection, other parts of the organization will be unavoidably modified; a changed part modifies other parts by modifying their functions (a moving equilibrium).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin quotations on correlated variation are cited. Physiological examples provided: unusual cerebral excitement affecting renal excretion; heart hypertrophy causing apoplexy and palsy; emotions affecting bile flow. The central question raised is whether such correlative modifications, when within normal limits, are inheritable—if they are, Darwin's correlated-variation statement is intelligible; if not, severe problems for selection-based accounts arise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological caution: absence of recognized evidence may reflect bias/inattention
rubrics_metrics.description: Lack of recognized evidence may be accounted for by inattention and reluctant attention; ignoring facts due to prevailing beliefs does not imply facts do not exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogies: initial rejection of pre-historic implements until geologists looked for them; general neglect of evidence for organic evolution before Darwin. Used to argue that observed scarcity of recorded instances of transmitted functionally-produced changes may be due to neglect rather than true absence.
